title: How I Optimized vLLM for High Concurrency in a Production Voice AI System

body:
In a recent production voice AI deployment, I used vLLM on a 3-node GPU cluster (6× GPUs: NVIDIA A4500 and A100) to serve a Qwen-based conversational model handling a high volume of simultaneous calls.

The system initially performed well under moderate load, but as concurrency increased, I started observing instability in KV-cache usage and request scheduling behavior.

The Problem I Observed in Production

vLLM provides useful internal telemetry, including:

  • Total GPU KV-cache capacity
  • Estimated maximum concurrency (for example, ~15x for long-context requests)
  • Preemption and recomputation events under memory pressure

At scale, I began seeing KV-cache preemption warnings as more sessions were added.

What this meant in practice:

  • Some active requests were temporarily paused
  • The system had to recompute partial states
  • Tail latency increased under load
  • Overall throughput became inconsistent during traffic spikes

This was a clear signal that the default memory and batching configuration was not optimized for our workload.

Scaling Across GPUs and Nodes

The first optimization step was horizontal scaling across GPUs using vLLM’s parallelism features.

I used a combination of:

  • Tensor parallelism (splitting model weights across GPUs)
  • Pipeline parallelism (splitting model layers across devices and nodes)

This allowed us to distribute Qwen across the full 3-node cluster.

Deployment Configuration

vllm serve Qwen/Qwen7B-Instruct \
  --tensor-parallel-size 3 \
  --pipeline-parallel-size 3 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8 \
  --port 8000

This setup effectively shards the model across multiple GPUs, reducing per-GPU memory pressure and freeing up more space for KV-cache allocation.

I also ensured low-latency interconnect performance by:

  • Using high-speed networking (100 GbE)
  • Enabling NCCL over InfiniBand where applicable
  • Configuring GPUDirect RDMA for faster GPU-to-GPU communication
  • Optimizing container shared memory (/dev/shm) for distributed workloads

This significantly reduced synchronization overhead across nodes.

Managing KV-Cache Pressure and Batching Behavior

Even after scaling out, KV-cache management remained the critical bottleneck.

I focused on tuning vLLM memory and scheduling parameters.

Key adjustments:

  • Increased GPU memory utilization to 0.8–0.9
  • Tuned continuous batching limits
  • Balanced throughput vs latency tradeoffs

Example configuration:

from vllm import LLM
llm = LLM(
    model="Qwen/Qwen7B-Instruct",
    tensor_parallel_size=3,
    pipeline_parallel_size=3,
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.8,
    max_num_batched_tokens=8192,
    max_num_seqs=8
)

What changed after tuning

  • Higher batching efficiency per iteration
  • More stable GPU utilization under load
  • Reduced KV-cache eviction events
  • Better throughput consistency during traffic spikes

I found that around 8000 max batched tokens provided the best balance between latency and throughput for our 8k context workload.

Chunked Prefill for Better GPU Utilization

I also leveraged vLLM’s chunked prefill mechanism.

Instead of processing long prompts in a single pass, the system splits them into smaller chunks and interleaves them with decoding tasks.

This improved:

  • GPU utilization balance between prefill and decode
  • Tail latency under heavy load
  • Stability during burst traffic scenarios

In production, this had a noticeable impact on smoothing out latency spikes.

Speculative Decoding for Latency Reduction

To further improve response times, we enabled speculative decoding.

This approach uses a smaller draft model to predict multiple tokens ahead, which are then verified by the main model.

Results:

  • Around 1.5x speedup with a draft model
  • Up to 2.8x speedup with prompt-based speculative decoding
  • Significant reduction in time-to-first-token under load

This was especially valuable for real-time voice AI scenarios where latency directly affects user experience.

KV-Cache Offloading for Extreme Concurrency

At peak load, I introduced KV-cache offloading using LMCache.

This allowed me to extend KV-cache capacity beyond GPU memory by spilling inactive cache states into CPU memory.

Benefits:

  • Reduced preemption events under extreme concurrency
  • Increased effective session capacity per GPU
  • Improved stability during traffic bursts

I allocated approximately 20 GB of CPU buffer per GPU in Kubernetes, which helped maintain session continuity without degrading performance.

Benchmarking and Validation

I validated all optimizations using vLLM serving benchmarks by simulating increasing concurrency levels.

Key metrics monitored:

  • Requests per second (RPS)
  • Token throughput
  • Inter-token latency
  • KV-cache usage
  • Preemption frequency

After tuning, I observed:

  • Significantly reduced preemption events
  • Higher stable concurrency limits
  • More predictable latency distribution under load

Final Production Outcome

After combining all optimizations, the system evolved from a constrained inference setup into a high-throughput real-time inference engine.

Key improvements:

  • Linear scalability across GPUs
  • Stable KV-cache behavior under high load
  • Reduced latency spikes during peak traffic
  • Higher sustained concurrency without recomputation overhead
